2611.18297.authors: Anthony Abou Mrad, Aviona Conti, Jayanth Pratap, Ruhika Iyer, Joseph Kim, King Shi, Yann Sakref, Luis M. Ahumada, Lisa Knowlton, Andrew M. Cameron, Khyzer Aziz, Jeffrey K. Jopling
2611.18297.abstract: AI judges, models that grade another system's output against a rubric, extend clinical review to the scale at which clinical AI writes. When teams use judge assessments to select a prompt or train a model, the judge becomes part of the intervention. Selection can then favor errors the judge overlooks. We describe what a judge's report must contain and the independent clinical test each judge-driven change needs.

2611.18531.title: Alignment by Socialization: Learning Tradeoffs Under Selection
2611.18531.authors: Thomas Brennan, Andrew W. Lo, Chaoyi Zhao
2611.18531.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) agents are expected to complete tasks while following rules of conduct, but these objectives can conflict. We study how evolutionary selection shapes an agent's choices between them, and whether experience can make those choices reflect human judgments and withstand subsequent pressures. In our model, copies of an agent face a common uncertain reward state, and only those taking the rewarded action reproduce. We show that long-run growth is maximized when each action is taken as often as the environment rewards it. We compare three policies. A task-only policy thrives in a sandbox rewarding completion alone but fails when conduct matters. A fixed linear policy increasingly favors task completion as its stakes rise, even where humans never reward it. A learned policy instead converges to the tradeoffs rewarded by its environment; when humans supply the rewards, we call this socialization. Accumulated experience makes socialization harder to reverse under subsequent task-only training, although violations can arise before the prevailing disposition changes, and finite memory weakens this protection. When a single violation can end a deployment, a hard prohibition can prevent it, but a mistaken prohibition can also be costly. Experiments with small neural networks illustrate how training targets and memory shape these outcomes. Our results suggest that alignment depends not only on the objectives assigned to agents, but also on the environments that shape and sustain their behavior.

2611.19292.title: Zero-Shot Weight-Space Programming for Prediction and Classification of Target Variables in Structured Datasets
2611.19292.abstract: Weight-space programming fixes every parameter of a feed-forward network by hand, with no gradient descent anywhere in the construction. Every demonstration so far starts from a target function handed to the model as a rule system, making it a compilation problem. A supervised dataset withholds that specification, so the procedure must do the statistical inference itself and then express the result in the parameterisation it was given. We ask whether a large language model can do both. It is shown a small dataset in full, with the architecture of a feed-forward network, and writes out every weight and bias as a literal number, with no optimizer, no gradient, no code execution, and no chance to evaluate it first. Each construction is sealed and pre-registers its expected score. The graded suite runs from two toy problems, through nine synthetic problems disguised by a hidden rotation, to the classical benchmarks and one real engineering regression. The frozen network matches the closed-form optimum wherever that optimum is linear, reaches the irreducible error of the generating process on three rungs where it is not, and beats every fitted baseline on two of those, including the same architecture trained by gradient descent. It fails on two rungs, both times because the structure to be found is oblique to the coordinates it analysed. Three further constructors separate two failure modes a single score conflates: one returns no parameter vector at all on the hardest rungs, another delivers everywhere while writing networks worse than predicting the mean. One of those failures proves avoidable: another constructor solves the oblique-hinge rung by a margin that survives multiple-comparison correction. What predicts whether the hidden layer earns its keep is the training error of a linear separator, which the composite complexity index misses.

2611.20794.title: Regularizing Treatment Leakage for LLM-based Uplift Estimation
2611.20794.authors: Bojing Feng, Jinqiu Deng, Zihan Hong, Yuan Xue, Wenqi Xiang, Shuhan Wang, Feng Xiao, Shiwei Wang, Zijiang Liu, Shaomin Li, Yongzhi Qi
2611.20794.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) provide semantic features for uplift estimation, but treatment-revealing text can induce prediction shortcuts that do not transfer to deployment. We propose LLM-based Uplift Leakage Regularization (LULR) to address this risk. With the LLM encoder frozen, LULR penalizes dependence between the causal head's trainable shared representation and treatment while retaining separate outcome heads. The penalty uses a variational approximation to the contrastive log-ratio upper bound (CLUB) of mutual information, targeting treatment dependence rather than generic parameter shrinkage. Controlled proxy experiments provide exploratory evidence of improved ranking scores under injected treatment information relative to no regularization and the tested weight-decay setting. Structured-only benchmarks show modest, dataset-dependent effects. On an industrial pricing randomized controlled trial, mean offline lift@0.3 is 0.258 for LULR, compared with 0.106 for the same-backbone baseline. A separate one-week online A/B test of the complete deployed pricing policy records 5.45% higher sales volume and 1.91% higher gross merchandise value than the control arm. These short-term policy-level gains do not isolate the regularizer's effect.

2611.22113.title: RegimeCouncil: Paired-Evidence Routing For Memory Conflict Governance In LLM Agents
2611.22113.authors: Qingcan Kang, Mingyang Liu, Shixiong Kai, Tao Zhong, Mingxuan Yuan
2611.22113.abstract: Alongside memory storage and retrieval, a fundamental challenge in long-term LLM agent systems is how the agent should act when stored memories conflict with an evolving world. Facts often go stale without explicit deletion, so the conflict surfaces before the store is refreshed: delayed feedback shows that acting on one outdated record hurt, but not whether suppression should stay on that fact (a local policy) or extend to other stored facts (a global policy). Existing systems hard-code one of these scopes at design time. We formulate this online choice, under hidden validity and delayed feedback, as memory conflict governance, and propose RegimeCouncil, a lightweight router that keeps both scopes as advisors and arbitrates between them without retraining the LLM. Each memory-assisted response is scored against a no-memory anchor, by off-path paired comparison or by inverse-propensity estimation from the executed action alone. A Local Advisor tracks only the queried fact, a Global Advisor pools recent outcomes across the store, and an asymmetric Meta Governor follows Local by default, switching to Global only when pooling yields a strictly positive recent utility margin. We prove that using delayed outcomes escapes the prompt-only regret floor, that neither fixed scope suffices alone, and that this margin gate switches within bounded time. On LongMemEval streams, historical drift in TempLAMA and TAQA, delays $\tau \in [1, 96]$, and sparse or bandit feedback, with Qwen3-30B-A3B and GPT-4o, RegimeCouncil outperforms the better fixed scope in all 30 held-out settings, by 5.2-7.3 points on disagreement episodes and +27.9 points over standalone cold-start fallback under clustered shifts, while cutting harmful stale-memory use at microsecond overhead.

2611.23910.title: MLE Agents: Autonomous ML Engineering in Large-scale Recommendation Systems
2611.23910.authors: Matthew Li, Albert Jiongqian Liang, Dilip Raj
2611.23910.abstract: The typical workflow for improving large-scale ranking and recommendation models is slow and tedious: an engineer forms a hypothesis, implements it as a code change, trains a model, and evaluates it both offline and online, often relying on their own intuition and experience along the way. Autonomous LLM agents promise to speed this up by running the loop on their own, but it is still unclear whether they can do this in industry-scale systems rather than on benchmarks or small proxy tasks. We build human-on-the-loop machine learning engineer (MLE) agents that propose, implement, train, and evaluate model changes on large-scale search rankers. Engineers retain control over objective design, search direction, and final-model review. We identify three obstacles that make this industry setting challenging: feedback takes hours per experiment, offline metrics do not always predict online impact, and improvements saturate after the early wins. We address these with parallel training runs, an objective calibrated to match online impact, and careful context engineering. In one campaign, the system ran 1,097 completed candidate experiments and accepted 325, a 29.6\% acceptance rate compared with 15.6\% in the earlier campaign under a different objective and search constraint. Its best model increases search volume by 0.23\% in an A/B test of large scale. Several improvements were architectural changes the team had never tried, drawn from the broader industry and literature, suggesting that MLE agents can explore regions of the design space that human intuition overlooks. We find that the design of the harness around the model matters: intuition suggests that a stronger underlying model is enough, but in our experience, the design of the loop around it is just as critical. More broadly, our work shows that autonomous agents can do real machine-learning engineering in industry-scale systems.

2611.24353.title: When Figures Disagree with Text: Evaluating Autonomous Visual Evidence Verification in Scientific Papers
2611.24353.authors: Guijia Zhang, Hongbo Qiu, Jiajun Zha, Guohao Cai, Hao Zheng, Huihao Jing, Kexu Cheng, Shipeng Luo, JinYang Huang, Shing-Chi Cheung, Changsheng Lu, Haoxuan Che, Harry Yang
2611.24353.abstract: Scientific figures carry evidence for the claims that cite them, so reviewing a paper means checking that a figure agrees with the text, and not only describing what the figure shows. Benchmarks of figure-text verification typically hand the model the figure, the claim, or the knowledge that an inconsistency exists, which leaves untested whether a model can find the figure worth checking in a complete paper, relate a visual element to the claim it conflicts with, and recognize the conflict. We study this autonomous setting on 31 full manuscripts, each carrying a reviewer-documented figure-text inconsistency from PRISMM-Bench that is hidden from the model. Six multimodal models review each PDF under a neutral prompt, and we then add one input at a time to the same manuscripts. Of 1,445 open-ended reviews, 60.6% mention the flawed figure, yet a grading rubric accepts only 3.3% as diagnosing its contradiction; a blind audit finds the rubric lenient, so we read these as rubric-accepted rates and compare conditions rather than absolute values. In a separate controlled run, naming the figure, without stating that it is flawed, raises rubric-accepted diagnosis from 4.3% to 20.4%, while a consistency instruction and coarse visual cues do not. When the contradiction is visible only in the rendered figure, text-only review yields no accepted diagnosis, while review of the rendered pages with the figure named reaches 15.8%. A baseline that lets the model choose which figures to check, ranked by centrality, stays at 4.8%. Deciding what to verify is thus a large part of the difficulty, and the selection rule we tested does not resolve it. Multimodal document understanding should be evaluated on whether a model can propose what to verify, not only answer questions about a figure it is handed.

2611.25613.title: Can an LLM Repair a Language Model in Weight Space Without Gradient Training?
2611.25613.authors: Bharath Kumar Bolla, Raghavender Surya Upadhayula, Vishnu Surya Reddy Nandi, Ramesh Nandipalli
2611.25613.abstract: Although an external language model can select and test repairs to another model's weights, behavior can also be recovered through fixed numerical edits. We assessed the value of interactive selection in a controlled study of Transformer repair. After inspecting predictions, activation summaries, and weight statistics, the editor selects projection recipes to apply to the target without gradient updates. We analyzed 20 recorded sessions involving five masked and causal language models, comparing the selected edits with fixed projections, scripted and matched-budget black-box search, and low-rank adaptation. Under the core two-layer fault, live selection matches black-box search on SmolLM2 and Qwen2.5. For Pythia, live selection achieves 65.62% completion accuracy, compared with 0% for black-box search and 66.15% for a fixed projection. Under a separate compound fault affecting attention and feed-forward weights, both scripted and LLM-guided selection increase the descriptive five-checkpoint mean from 24.89% to 71.25% using the same operator family. On unmodified checkpoints, scripted projection yields small gains or losses on a separate set of framed questions. The experiments identify cases in which feedback changes an edit decision, operator coverage accounts for recovery, or supervised adaptation performs better. Combined with measurements of parameter restoration and preservation, these comparisons establish the scope of controller-guided repair for the tested faults and completion tasks.

2611.26538.title: LLM GerryMandering: Separating Interactions from Additive Effects in LLM Audits
2611.26538.authors: George Rahul, Ronit Jalihal, Bhaskara Hanuma Vedula, Ponnurangam Kumaraguru, Pushkar Shukla
2611.26538.abstract: Intersectional bias arises when a model treats people who hold several marginalised identities at once differently from what their separate identities would predict. Auditing such intersectional subgroups remains a challenge: their number grows quadratically, and there is no agreed baseline for what independent attributes would predict. Without such a baseline, many existing audits flag a subgroup when it exceeds each attribute alone, a condition that attributes acting independently already satisfy. We test this standard criterion on 150 synthetic datasets built with no interaction. With the shuffle null, it flags 66.1 false subgroups per dataset on average, and at least one in every dataset. When we plant interactions of known size into these datasets, a repaired null lets the criterion recover only 32% of them. We introduce ADDIS (Additive Intersectional Screen), which fits an additive model over all attributes, scores each subgroup by its Additive Residual Distance (ARD) from that model's prediction, and tests it against a Freedman-Lane null. On our synthetic benchmark, ADDIS flags 0.09 false subgroups per dataset and recovers 84% of the same planted interactions. We then build IndiPersona, 10,000 synthetic Indian personas with six identity attributes, and audit 13 open language models. The standard criterion flags 7.1% of the 738 tested subgroups on average; ADDIS flags 3.0%. Gender identity crossed with sexual orientation is the largest pairing in every model, and counterfactual personas confirm it and additionally reveal a caste x class interaction in all but one model that the observational test lacked the data to detect. Much of what audits report as intersectional bias can thus arise from independent single-attribute effects alone, yet a small core of interactions survives.

2309.03876.title: OpinionGPT: Modelling Explicit Biases in Instruction-Tuned LLMs
2309.03876.authors: Patrick Haller, Ansar Aynetdinov, Alan Akbik
2309.03876.abstract: Instruction-tuned Large Language Models (LLMs) have recently showcased remarkable ability to generate fitting responses to natural language instructions. However, an open research question concerns the inherent biases of trained models and their responses. For instance, if the data used to tune an LLM is dominantly written by persons with a specific political bias, we might expect generated answers to share this bias. Current research work seeks to de-bias such models, or suppress potentially biased answers. With this demonstration, we take a different view on biases in instruction-tuning: Rather than aiming to suppress them, we aim to make them explicit and transparent. To this end, we present OpinionGPT, a web demo in which users can ask questions and select all biases they wish to investigate. The demo will answer this question using a model fine-tuned on text representing each of the selected biases, allowing side-by-side comparison. To train the underlying model, we identified 11 different biases (political, geographic, gender, age) and derived an instruction-tuning corpus in which each answer was written by members of one of these demographics. This paper presents OpinionGPT, illustrates how we trained the bias-aware model and showcases the web application (available at https://opiniongpt.informatik.hu-berlin.de).

2409.01382.title: Automatic Detection of LLM-Generated Code: A Comparative Case Study of Contemporary Models Across Function and Class Granularities
2409.01382.authors: Musfiqur Rahman, SayedHassan Khatoonabadi, Ahmad Abdellatif, Emad Shihab
2409.01382.abstract: The adoption of Large Language Models (LLMs) for code generation risks incorporating vulnerable code into software systems. Existing detectors face two critical limitations: a lack of systematic cross-model validation and opaque "black box" operation. We address this through a comparative study of code generated by four distinct LLMs: GPT-3.5, Claude 3 Haiku, Claude Haiku 4.5, and GPT-OSS. Analyzing 14,485 Python functions and 11,913 classes from the CodeSearchNet dataset, we generated corresponding code with all four LLMs. Using interpretable software metrics, we trained CatBoost classifiers for each configuration. Our analysis reveals that granularity effects dominate model differences by a factor of 8.6, with negligible feature overlap, indicating that function-level and class-level detection rely on fundamentally disjoint structural signatures. We discover critical granularity-dependent inversions: while modern models (Claude, GPT-OSS) are more detectable at the class level, GPT-3.5 is an anomaly that uniquely excels at the function level. SHAP analysis identifies the Comment-to-Code Ratio as the sole universal discriminator. However, its predictive magnitude varies drastically across models, explaining why detectors trained on specific LLMs fail to generalize. Our findings demonstrate that GPT-3.5's exceptional detectability (AUC-ROC 0.96) is unrepresentative of contemporary models (AUC-ROC approximately between 0.68 and 0.80). Robust detection requires moving beyond single-model studies to account for substantial diversity in structural fingerprints across architectures and granularities.

2410.24035.title: A context-adaptive policy framework for robust and reactive robotic manipulation via uncertainty-aware imitation learning
2410.24035.authors: Tim R. Winter, Leonard Kl\"upfel, Ashok M. Sundaram, Werner Friedl, Maximo A. Roa, Freek Stulp, Jo\~ao Silv\'erio
2410.24035.abstract: Generating robust and reactive manipulation strategies that can adapt to changing context information is a challenging task in robotics. Over the years, Learning from Demonstration (LfD) has emerged as an intuitive and effective solution for generating reactive policies, particularly by following dynamical-system(DS)-based approaches. However, most state-of-the-art DS-based approaches focus on addressing the robustness limitations, overlooking the modulation of policies in response to the environment. As a result, they tend to be inflexible with respect to parameterization by task-dependent variables. In this work, we build on existing work on policy fusion and uncertainty quantification to propose a context-adaptive policy framework that combines task-parameterized, robust and reactive manipulation. For this, we use LfD to acquire a policy that is conditioned on the robot state and low-dimensional task-dependent parameters reflecting the environment. We combine the learned policy with additional uncertainty-aware policies using a Mixture of Experts (MoE) formulation to improve its out-of-distribution (OOD) robustness and convergence behavior. The approach is evaluated on the LASA handwriting dataset and on a real 7-DoF robot in three scenarios: force-conditioned grasping, manipulation of deformable food items and object-centric grasping.

2502.05085.title: Causality can systematically address the monsters under the bench(marks)
2502.05085.authors: Felix Leeb, Zhijing Jin, Bernhard Sch\"olkopf
2502.05085.abstract: Effective and reliable evaluation is essential for advancing empirical machine learning. However, the increasing accessibility of generalist models and the progress towards ever more complex, high-level tasks make systematic evaluation more challenging. Benchmarks are plagued by various biases, artifacts, or leakage, while models may behave unreliably due to poorly explored failure modes. Haphazard treatments and inconsistent formulations of such "monsters" leads to a duplication of efforts, a lack of trust in results, and unsupported inferences. In this position paper, we argue causality offers an ideal framework to systematically address these challenges. By making causal assumptions in an approach explicit, we can faithfully model phenomena, formulate testable hypotheses with explanatory power, and leverage principled tools for analysis. To make the design of conceptual causal models more accessible, we identify several useful Common Abstract Topologies (CATs) in causal graphs which help gain insight into the reasoning abilities in large language models. Through a series of case studies, we demonstrate how the precise yet pragmatic language of causality clarifies the strengths and limitations of a method and inspires new approaches for systematic progress.

2505.22976.title: LoopNav: Benchmarking Spatial Consistency in World Models
2505.22976.authors: Kewei Lian, Shaofei Cai, Yitao Liang, Anji Liu
2505.22976.abstract: The ability to simulate the world in a spatially consistent manner is a crucial requirement for effective world models. Such a model enables high-quality visual generation, and also ensures the reliability of world models for downstream tasks such as simulation and planning. It must not only retain long-horizon observational information, but also enables the construction of explicit or implicit internal spatial representations. However, existing datasets do not explicitly enforce spatial consistency constraints, limiting both the ability to systematically evaluate this capability and to learn it through data-driven approaches. Furthermore, most existing benchmarks primarily emphasize visual coherence or generation quality, neglecting the requirement of long-range spatial consistency. To bridge this gap, we propose LoopNav, a dataset and corresponding benchmark centered on loop-based navigation for evaluating spatial consistency. The dataset comprises 200 hours of loop-based navigation videos with actions, collected from diverse locations in the open-world environment of Minecraft. We further introduce a Scene Graph Consistency Score(SGCS) to quantify spatial consistency while remaining invariant to pixel-level variations. Dataset, benchmark, and code are open-sourced to support future research.

2505.23331.title: Fine-Tuning Next-Scale Visual Autoregressive Models with Group Relative Policy Optimization
2505.23331.authors: Matteo Gallici, Haitz S\'aez de Oc\'ariz Borde
2505.23331.abstract: Fine-tuning pre-trained generative models with Reinforcement Learning (RL) has emerged as an effective approach for aligning outputs more closely with nuanced human preferences. In this paper, we investigate the application of Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to fine-tune next-scale visual autoregressive (VAR) models. Our empirical results demonstrate that this approach enables alignment to intricate reward signals derived from aesthetic predictors and CLIP embeddings, significantly enhancing image quality and enabling precise control over the generation style. Interestingly, by leveraging CLIP, our method can help VAR models generalize beyond their initial ImageNet distribution: through RL-driven exploration, these models can generate images aligned with prompts referencing image styles that were absent during pre-training. In summary, we show that RL-based fine-tuning is both efficient and effective for VAR models, benefiting particularly from their fast inference speeds, which are advantageous for online sampling, an aspect that poses significant challenges for diffusion-based alternatives.

2509.04588.title: Beyond Output Faithfulness: Diagnosing and Mitigating Pathway Rerouting in Feature Attribution
2509.04588.abstract: Insertion and deletion are standard metrics for evaluating feature attributions by progressively adding or removing pixels. While they test whether attributed features control a model output, they do not verify whether they do so through the computation that supports the clean prediction. We study this distinction with Ensemble Quantile Optimization (EQO), a differentiable method that directly optimizes the insertion sequence. On CNNs, Unconstrained EQO attains the highest insertion scores while departing from clean representations and retaining its insertion score after channels supporting the clean prediction are ablated. Together, these results reveal pathway rerouting that output-only metrics cannot detect. On a Vision Transformer, target predictions from black inputs and attention deviation expose the same failure. To address this, we introduce ClipGrad, a layer-wise gradient filter that preserves clean activation trajectories during optimization. ClipGrad suppresses rerouting exploits while maintaining high output sensitivity across convolutional networks and Vision Transformers, and token intervention confirms this mitigation on the Transformer. These results show that output sensitivity is necessary but insufficient: a faithful attribution must control the output through internal computation used for the clean prediction.

2509.07295.title: Reconstruction Alignment Improves Unified Multimodal Models
2509.07295.authors: Ji Xie, Trevor Darrell, Luke Zettlemoyer, XuDong Wang
2509.07295.abstract: We discover a simple but effective way for visual understanding to help visual generation in a unified model. Unified multimodal models (UMMs) unify visual understanding and generation within a single architecture. However, conventional training relies on image-text pairs (or sequences) whose captions are typically sparse and miss fine-grained visual details, even when they use hundreds of words to describe a simple image. We introduce Reconstruction Alignment (RecA), a resource-efficient post-training method that leverages visual understanding encoder embeddings as dense "text prompts," providing rich supervision without captions. Concretely, RecA conditions a UMM on its own visual understanding embeddings and optimizes it to reconstruct the input image with a self-supervised reconstruction loss, thereby using visual understanding to improve image generation. Despite its simplicity, RecA is broadly applicable: across autoregressive, masked-autoregressive, and diffusion-based UMMs, it consistently improves generation and editing fidelity. With only 27 GPU hours, post-training with RecA substantially improves image generation performance on GenEval (0.73 $\rightarrow$ 0.90) and DPGBench (80.93 $\rightarrow$ 88.15), while also boosting editing benchmarks (ImgEdit 3.38 $\rightarrow$ 3.75, GEdit 6.94 $\rightarrow$ 7.27). Notably, RecA surpasses much larger open-source models and applies broadly across diverse UMM architectures, establishing it as an efficient and general post-training alignment strategy for UMMs.

2510.02848.title: Rhythm-TTS: High-Fidelity Shortcut Latent Modeling and Probabilistic Rhythm Generation for Zero-Shot Text-to-Speech
2510.02848.authors: Hieu-Nghia Huynh-Nguyen, Ngoc-Son Nguyen, Long-Khanh Pham, Huynh Nguyen Dang, Huy Tien Nguyen, Van Nguyen
2510.02848.abstract: Zero-shot text-to-speech (TTS) systems are commonly built on either discrete codec tokens or continuous acoustic representations. Discrete-token models benefit from stable sequence modeling and explicit speech factorization, but they ultimately synthesize speech through codebook lookup and codeword composition, which can accumulate errors and impose a quality ceiling on naturalness and speaker similarity. Continuous-representation models can generate fine-grained speech latents directly, but often require heavier in-context modeling and less explicit alignment. This paper presents Rhythm-TTS, a shortcut zero-shot TTS framework that combines the factorizability of discrete codec tokens with the fidelity of continuous latent generation. Instead of using predicted codec tokens as the final acoustic representation, Rhythm-TTS uses them as a semantic-acoustic prior and directly generates holistic continuous speech latents with flow matching, bypassing the discrete-to-latent reconstruction path at inference time. We further address an underexplored dimension of speech naturalness: rhythm diversity across multiple synthesis runs. Motivated by the hypothesis that rhythm variation is largely governed by phoneme duration changes and the occurrence of silent pauses, we introduce probabilistic Duration and Silence Generators to sample dynamic pacing patterns before acoustic generation. Experiments on zero-shot TTS benchmarks evaluate intelligibility, naturalness, speaker similarity, efficiency, and run-to-run rhythm diversity, showing that the proposed shortcut latent modeling and probabilistic rhythm generation improve the fidelity and temporal naturalness of non-autoregressive zero-shot TTS. Code and audio samples are available at our demo page https://rhythm-tts.github.io.

2510.04392.title: Improving Consistency in Retrieval-Augmented Systems with Group Similarity Rewards
2510.04392.authors: Faisal Hamman, Chenyang Zhu, Anoop Kumar, Xujun Peng, Sanghamitra Dutta, Daben Liu, Alfy Samuel
2510.04392.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems are increasingly deployed in high-stakes domains where users expect outputs to be consistent across semantically equivalent queries. However, existing systems often exhibit significant inconsistencies due to variability in both the retriever and generator, undermining trust and reliability. In this work, we focus on information consistency, i.e., the requirement that generated outputs convey the same core content across semantically equivalent inputs. We introduce a principled evaluation framework that decomposes RAG consistency into retriever-level, generator-level, and end-to-end components, enabling systematic identification of inconsistency sources. To improve consistency, we propose Paraphrased Set Group Relative Policy Optimization (PS-GRPO), an RL approach that leverages multiple rollouts across paraphrased set to assign group similarity rewards. We leverage PS-GRPO to achieve Information Consistent RAG (Con-RAG), training the generator to produce consistent outputs across paraphrased queries and remain robust to retrieval-induced variability. Because exact reward computation over paraphrase sets is computationally expensive, we also introduce a scalable approximation method that retains effectiveness while enabling efficient, large-scale training. Empirical evaluations across short-form, multi-hop, and long-form QA benchmarks demonstrate that Con-RAG significantly improves consistency while preserving accuracy compared to baselines, even in the absence of explicit ground-truth supervision. Our work provides practical solutions for evaluating and building reliable RAG systems for safety-critical deployments.

2510.05310.title: RAG Makes Guardrails Brittle? Investigating Robustness of Guardrails under RAG-style Contexts
2510.05310.authors: Yining She, Daniel W. Peterson, Marianne Menglin Liu, Vikas Upadhyay, Mohammad Hossein Chaghazardi, Eunsuk Kang, Dan Roth
2510.05310.abstract: With the increasing adoption of large language models (LLMs), ensuring the safety of LLM systems has become a pressing concern. External LLM-based guardrail models have emerged as a popular solution to screen unsafe inputs and outputs, but they are themselves fine-tuned or prompt-engineered LLMs vulnerable to data distribution shifts. In this paper, taking Retrieval Augmentation Generation (RAG) as a case study, we investigate how robust LLM-based guardrails are against additional information embedded in the context. Through a systematic evaluation of 3 Llama Guards and 2 GPT-oss models, we find that inserting benign retrieved documents flips the judgments of input and output guardrails in around 11% and 8% of cases respectively, with the majority of these flips (72% and 64%) reversing previously correct decisions. We further analyze the effect of each component in the augmented context: retrieved documents, user query, and LLM response. Two tested mitigations reveal that the robustness gap is not easily closed. These results expose a context-robustness gap in current guardrails.

2510.06637.title: Learning to Assimilate: Amortized Control for Autoregressive Diffusion
2510.06637.authors: Prakhar Srivastava, Farrin Marouf Sofian, Francesco Immorlano, Kushagra Pandey, Stephan Mandt
2510.06637.abstract: Autoregressive diffusion models (ARDMs) offer expressive priors for forecasting chaotic dynamics. However, maintaining consistency with sparse observations over long rollouts can require substantial test-time computation. We introduce Control-Augmented Data Assimilation (CADA), which trains a lightweight controller on top of a frozen ARDM to steer predictions toward future observations. Using a KL-regularized stochastic optimal control objective, the controller learns from short autoregressive rollouts to anticipate observations while staying close to the pretrained dynamics. At inference, it injects corrections at each denoising step without per-forecast optimization. Across two chaotic PDE benchmarks, CADA improves long-horizon accuracy, stability, and physical fidelity under sparse observations. On compact ERA5, it outperforms diffusion-based baselines in most regimes with over $10\times$ faster inference than conditional diffusion baselines. Applied to frozen GenCast, CADA also reduces temperature errors across 12--48-hour forecasts with spatially sparse observations. Code is available at https://github.com/mandt-lab/cada.

2510.14581.title: Provable Selective Auto-labeling with Reliability Guarantees
2510.14581.authors: Huipeng Huang, Wenbo Liao, Huajun Xi, Hao Zeng, Mengchen Zhao, Hongxin Wei
2510.14581.abstract: Auto-labeling has emerged as a popular, cost-effective alternative to manual annotation. However, its performance is often highly inconsistent across different tasks, underscoring the importance of selective strategies. Despite this, existing heuristic methods for selective auto-labeling still rely heavily on model confidence scores and offer no reliable guarantee on the trustworthiness of the selected examples. To address this, we propose \textbf{Conformal Labeling}, a novel method that selects a subset of auto-generated labels with a provably controlled false labeling rate (FLR). Our key idea is to formulate selective auto-labeling as a multiple-hypothesis testing problem, where each hypothesis indicates whether to accept the auto-generated label for an instance. Specifically, we construct a conformal $p$-value for each auto-generated label using a small calibration set, and then employ the Benjamini--Hochberg (BH) procedure with a novel correction factor to construct the subset with guaranteed FLR control. Theoretically, we show that our method achieves finite-sample FLR control and asymptotically optimal statistical power among all $p$-value thresholding rules. Extensive experiments on classification and open-ended generation tasks validate the effectiveness of our method, achieving high statistical power while strictly controlling the FLR.

2511.00086.title: Generalizing Test-time Compute-optimal Scaling as an Optimizable Graph
2511.00086.authors: Fali Wang, Jihai Chen, Shuhua Yang, Runxue Bao, Tianxiang Zhao, Zhiwei Zhang, Xianfeng Tang, Hui Liu, Qi He, Suhang Wang
2511.00086.abstract: Test-Time Scaling (TTS) improves large language models (LLMs) by allocating additional computation during inference, typically through parallel, sequential, or hybrid scaling. However, prior studies often assume fixed collaboration architectures (e.g., topologies) and single-model usage, overlooking that optimal architectures and model combinations can vary across tasks. Therefore, we study the novel problem of searching for compute-optimal model combinations and architectures in TTS under a fixed budget. We formalize it as a multi-LLM collaboration graph, where nodes encode roles and LLM model assignments, and edges capture information flow. This problem is challenging because (i) the combinatorial search space is prohibitively large, and (ii) task-specific requirements demand tailored designs. To address these, we reformulate the problem as probabilistic graph optimization and, through pilot experiments, derive three empirical insights into TTS collaboration graphs. Guided by these insights, we propose Agent-REINFORCE, an LLM-agent-augmented framework that mirrors the REINFORCE pipeline by mapping sampling-gradient-update to sampling-feedback-update, where feedback serves as a textual gradient to update the probabilistic graph and efficiently search for optimal multi-LLM collaboration graphs. Experiments show that Agent-REINFORCE outperforms both traditional and LLM-based baselines in sample efficiency and search performance, and effectively identifies optimal graphs under joint objectives of accuracy and inference latency.

2511.14262.title: Object-Centric World Models for Causality-Aware Reinforcement Learning
2511.14262.abstract: World models have been developed to support sample-efficient deep reinforcement learning agents. However, it remains challenging for world models to accurately replicate environments that are high-dimensional, non-stationary, and composed of multiple objects with rich interactions since most world models learn holistic representations of all environmental components. By contrast, humans perceive the environment by decomposing it into discrete objects, facilitating efficient decision-making. Motivated by this insight, we propose \emph{Slot Transformer Imagination with CAusality-aware reinforcement learning} (STICA), a unified framework in which object-centric Transformers serve as the world model and causality-aware policy and value networks. STICA represents each observation as a set of object-centric tokens, together with tokens for the agent action and the resulting reward, enabling the world model to predict token-level dynamics and interactions. The policy and value networks then estimate token-level cause--effect relations and use them in the attention layers, yielding causality-guided decision-making. Experiments on object-rich benchmarks demonstrate that STICA consistently outperforms state-of-the-art agents in both sample efficiency and final performance.

2511.17450.title: Verify Before You Generate: Sketch-Guided Efficient Motion-Planning for Video Generation
2511.17450.authors: Yidong Huang, Zun Wang, Han Lin, Dong-Ki Kim, Shayegan Omidshafiei, Jaehong Yoon, Yue Zhang, Mohit Bansal
2511.17450.abstract: Recent video generation approaches increasingly rely on planning intermediate control signals like object trajectories to improve temporal coherence and motion fidelity. However, these methods mostly employ single-shot plans that are typically limited to simple motion instructions, leading to suboptimal motion quality, or iterative refinement which requires multiple calls to the video generator and incurs high computational cost. To address this trade-off, we propose SketchVerify, a training-free framework whose key insight is to verify motion plans using lightweight video sketches before invoking the expensive video generator. This lightweight planning space enables efficient comparison of multiple candidate trajectories and bounded iterative refinement before a single final video-generation pass. Given a prompt and a reference image, SketchVerify samples multiple candidate trajectories and renders each as a lightweight video sketch by compositing the moving objects over a static background. A vision-language verifier then ranks these sketches according to instruction alignment and visual motion consistency, allowing unsuitable trajectories to be rejected before full video synthesis. The motion plan is iteratively refined until a satisfactory one is identified, then passed to a trajectory-conditioned generator for final synthesis. Experiments on WORLDMODELBENCH and PHYWORLDBENCH demonstrate consistent improvements in instruction following and temporally coherent, visually plausible motion. Using the same ATI-14B generator, SketchVerify improves the aggregate WorldModelBench score from 7.71 to 8.71. Compared with full-video iterative refinement, it achieves a 13.1x planning-stage speedup and a 3.6x end-to-end speedup.

2601.06222.title: Learning and Comparing Local Traces for Weakly Supervised Image Manipulation Localization
2601.06222.authors: Xinghao Wang, Changtao Miao, Dianmo Sheng, Tao Gong, Qi Chu, Nenghai Yu, Quanchen Zou, Deyue Zhang, Xiangzheng Zhang
2601.06222.abstract: Image manipulation localization identifies edited regions and provides spatial evidence for assessing image reliability, but fully supervised methods require costly pixel-level annotations. Weakly supervised methods reduce this cost using image-level labels, but classification can rely on a few salient cues without ensuring accurate or complete localization. This difficulty is pronounced when manipulation traces are weak and unevenly distributed and authentic and manipulated regions share similar appearance. We propose a CLIP-based framework that integrates Trace-Oriented Vision--Language Adaptation (TOVA) and Relation-Aware Trace Discrimination (RATD). TOVA adapts the visual encoder and uses global visual context to aggregate edge-weighted patch features into image-conditioned class prompts. The resulting class representations support image-level alignment and guide patch selection for Hierarchical Trace Contrastive Learning, providing local contrastive supervision across visual layers. RATD combines local context, spatial structure, and original-image details, then compares learned descriptors between appearance-matched regions. Bidirectional comparison messages are integrated with local features for dense localization. The two components share a visual encoder and are jointly trained using only image-level authenticity labels. Experiments on multiple public benchmarks demonstrate that our framework outperforms the evaluated weakly supervised baselines in image manipulation localization.

2602.01990.title: SAME: Stabilized Mixture-of-Experts for Multimodal Continual Instruction Tuning
2602.01990.authors: Zhen-Hao Xie, Jun-Tao Tang, Yu-Cheng Shi, Han-Jia Ye, De-Chuan Zhan, Da-Wei Zhou
2602.01990.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) achieve strong performance through instruction tuning, but real-world deployment requires them to continually expand their capabilities, making Multimodal Continual Instruction Tuning (MCIT) essential. Recent methods leverage sparse expert routing to promote task specialization, but we find that the expert routing process suffers from drift as the data distribution evolves. For example, a grounding query that previously activated localization experts may instead be routed to irrelevant experts after learning OCR tasks. Meanwhile, the grounding-related experts can be overwritten by new tasks and lose their original functionality. Such failure reflects two problems: router drift, where expert selection becomes inconsistent over time, and expert drift, where shared experts are overwritten across tasks. Therefore, we propose StAbilized Mixture-of-Experts (SAME) for MCIT. To address router drift, SAME stabilizes expert selection by decomposing routing dynamics into orthogonal subspaces and updating only task-relevant directions. To mitigate expert drift, we regulate expert updates via curvature-aware scaling using historical input covariance in a rehearsal-free manner. SAME also introduces adaptive expert activation to freeze selected experts during training, reducing redundant computation and cross-task interference. We also introduce a new benchmark to evaluate MCIT with long task sequence, and extensive experiments demonstrate SAME's SOTA performance. Code is available at https://github.com/LAMDA-CL/Prism.

2602.02523.title: TabularMath: Evaluating Computational Extrapolation in Tabular Learning via Program-Verified Synthesis
2602.02523.authors: Zerui Cheng, Jiashuo Liu, Jianzhu Yao, Pramod Viswanath, Ge Zhang, Wenhao Huang
2602.02523.abstract: Standard tabular benchmarks reward interpolation: predicting values inside the data manifold, where local statistical smoothing works. However, much high-value tabular data, from pricing and financial rules to physical simulation, is produced by deterministic computations rather than noisy relationships. Can tabular models move from statistical interpolation to computational extrapolation, returning exact answers even beyond the range seen in training? We introduce TabularMath, a benchmark of 114 deterministic computations (233,472 rows) compiled from GSM8K and AIME problems into verified programs. We evaluate nine tabular methods, closed-form and symbolic regression baselines, and in-context learning with GPT-OSS-120B. On regression metrics, TabPFN v2.5 looks excellent: with 128 rows its median $R^2$ is 0.999 in-distribution, and it is the only tabular method whose median $R^2$ stays positive (0.76) when nearly every answer exceeds the training range. Exact answers tell a different story. Out of distribution (OOD), its accuracy falls from 39.5% to 7.8%, it answers no query correctly in 70 of 100 GSM8K tasks, and sixteen times more rows raise its OOD accuracy by only 0.4 points. Yet the answers are in the table: by construction, every label is a program's output on the row's inputs, and the training rows typically suffice to recover that program. Symbolic regression on the numbers alone recovers every OOD answer in 72 of 100 GSM8K tasks, and in-context learning with GPT-OSS-120B answers 39.2% of OOD queries. Tabular foundation models fit the trend but miss the computation, an inductive-bias gap that more data does not close. The competition-level AIME tasks remain open for every method.

2602.04417.title: EMA Policy Gradient: Taming Reinforcement Learning for LLMs with EMA Anchor and Top-k KL
2602.04417.abstract: Reinforcement Learning (RL) has enabled Large Language Models (LLMs) to acquire increasingly complex reasoning and agentic behaviors. In this work, we propose two simple techniques to improve policy gradient algorithms for LLMs. First, we replace the fixed anchor policy during RL with an Exponential Moving Average (EMA), similar to a target network in deep Q-learning. Second, we introduce Top-$k$ KL estimator, which allows for flexible interpolation between exact KL and sampled KL. We derive the stability conditions for using EMA anchor; moreover, we show that our Top-$k$ KL estimator yields both unbiased KL values and unbiased gradients at any $k$, while bringing the benefits of exact KL. When combined with GRPO, the two techniques (EMA-PG) lead to a significant performance boost. On math reasoning, it allows R1-distilled Qwen-1.5B to reach 53.9% on OlympiadBench compared to 50.8% by GRPO. On agentic RL domains, with Qwen-3B base, EMA-PG improves GRPO by an average of 35.6% across 7 datasets of Q&A with search engines, including 29.7% $\rightarrow$ 45.8% on HotpotQA, 27.4% $\rightarrow$ 40.5% on 2WikiMultiHopQA. Overall, we show that EMA-PG is a simple, principled, and powerful approach to scaling RL for LLMs. Code: https://github.com/LunjunZhang/ema-pg

2603.11842.title: The Landscape of Generative AI in Information Systems: A Synthesis of Secondary Reviews and Research Agendas
2603.11842.authors: Aleksander Jarz\k{e}bowicz, Adam Przyby{\l}ek, Jacinto Estima, Yen Ying Ng, Jakub Swacha, Beata Zielosko, Lech Madeyski, Noel Carroll, Kai-Kristian Kemell, Bartosz Marcinkowski, Alberto Rodrigues da Silva, Viktoria Stray, Netta Iivari, Anh Nguyen-Duc, Jorge Melegati, Boris Deliba\v{s}i\'c, Emilio Insfran
2603.11842.abstract: The post-ChatGPT surge has rapidly reframed IS research and practice. As organizations and society grapple with GenAI adoption, a body of secondary studies and research agendas has emerged to synthesize early evidence and chart directions for future inquiry. This study reviews secondary and roadmap papers to synthesize the state of knowledge on GenAI's benefits and challenges in IS, and to identify future research directions. We performed a systematic search across Scopus, WoS, and eAIS for publications from 2023 onwards. Following a rigorous, multi-stage screening process, we selected a final set of 28 papers for analysis using bibliometric mapping and thematic analysis. We also conducted a quality assessment of all sources to gauge confidence in each source's contribution to the findings. GenAI offers transformative potential to drive productivity, accelerate innovation, personalize services, and democratize access to expertise. However, its adoption is constrained by interrelated challenges: technical unreliability, societal-ethical risks, and a governance vacuum. Interpreted through a socio-technical lens, our findings reveal a persistent misalignment between GenAI's fast-evolving technical subsystem and the slower-adapting social subsystem, positioning IS research as critical for achieving joint optimization. To bridge this gap, we propose a research agenda that reorients IS scholarship from analyzing impacts toward actively shaping the co-evolution of technical capabilities with organizational routines, societal values, and regulatory institutions: emphasizing hybrid human-AI ensembles, situated validation, design principles for probabilistic systems, and adaptive governance. For practitioners and policymakers, responsible adoption requires balancing automation with human augmentation alongside transparent governance and adaptive regulations to ensure broadly shared benefits.

2603.20521.title: Delightful Policy Gradient under Distributed Friction
2603.20521.abstract: Distributed reinforcement learning trains on data from stale, buggy, or mismatched actors, whose actions often have high surprisal (negative log-probability) under the learner's policy. Supervised fine-tuning learns stably from such logged data, while policy gradient often does not. We trace the difference to negative learning from surprising data: rare failures can dominate finite-batch updates, while rare successes carry information the current policy would otherwise miss. The Delightful Policy Gradient (DG) separates the two by gating each term with delight, the product of advantage and surprisal, and needs no behavior probabilities. In a contaminated bandit, DG suppresses the perpendicular noise of rare failures by a factor that vanishes as the learner improves; no gate based only on learner probability can do this without also suppressing rare successes. On MNIST with stale actors, DG beats importance-weighted policy gradient given the exact behavior probabilities. On a transformer sequence task, DG often reaches an order of magnitude lower error under staleness, actor--learner probability mismatch, actor bugs, reward corruption, and rare discovery. With four frictions combined, its sample-efficiency advantage grows with sequence length. All experiments are controlled diagnostics; we do not evaluate an end-to-end distributed system.

2603.20526.title: Does This Gradient Spark Joy?
2603.20526.abstract: Policy gradient computes a backward pass for every sample, although the backward pass is expensive and most samples carry little learning value. The Delightful Policy Gradient (DG) scores learning value in the forward pass with \emph{delight}, the product of advantage and surprisal (negative log-probability). We introduce the \emph{Kondo gate}, which compares delight against a compute price and pays for a backward pass only when the sample is worth it; sweeping the price traces a quality--cost trade-off. On MNIST, keeping 3\% of gradient terms learns faster than standard policy gradient even when backward passes are free, and nearly matches full DG. In bandits, zero-price gating preserves the expected gradient direction and removes its perpendicular noise, delight ranks samples more reliably than additive mixes of value and surprise, and a rare action with high reward variance marks where delight fails. On transformer token reversal, the gate's advantage grows with sequence length and vocabulary size. Because delight tolerates moderate noise, a cheap approximate forward pass could screen samples before expensive backpropagation, a training analogue of speculative decoding.

2603.25063.title: TopoPilot: Reliable Conversational Workflow Automation for Topological Data Analysis and Visualization
2603.25063.authors: Nathaniel Gorski, Shusen Liu, Bei Wang
2603.25063.abstract: Recent agentic systems demonstrate that large language models can generate complex codebases from natural language prompts. Despite this progress, they present reliability concerns for scientific visualization due to invalid operations, subtle errors, and failure to resolve underspecified inputs. In this work, we introduce TopoPilot, a reliable and extensible agentic framework for automating complex scientific visualization workflows. We focus on topological data analysis and visualization as a primary use case, while designing the framework to generalize to broader visualization domains. TopoPilot employs a two-agent architecture: an orchestrator translates user prompts into workflows composed of atomic backend actions, while a verifier evaluates workflows prior to execution. Its modular design isolates components and supports new topological descriptors and domain-specific workflows without modifying the core system. It also employs numerous deterministic guardrails to ensure semantic consistency and accurate execution. To systematically improve reliability, we develop a taxonomy of failure modes and employ targeted safeguards for each class of error. Across 2,000 simulated multi-turn conversations spanning 100 prompts, including adversarial and infeasible requests, TopoPilot achieves a success rate exceeding 95%, compared with under 50% for a baseline without comprehensive guardrails and verification. We also show that TopoPilot outperforms Claude Code and Codex on similar prompts in terms of accuracy, completion time, and token usage.

2604.14016.title: The Projector Forgets Too: Joint Merging for Multimodal Continual Instruction Tuning
2604.14016.authors: Zijian Gao, Wangwang Jia, Xingxing Zhang, Pengfei Qian, Tao Sun, Bo Ding, Yong Dou, Zhen Huang, Dongsheng Li, Huaimin Wang, Kele Xu
2604.14016.abstract: Multimodal Continual Instruction Tuning (MCIT) is essential for sequential task adaptation of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) but is severely restricted by catastrophic forgetting. While existing literature focuses on the reasoning language backbone, in this work, we find that forgetting can arise from changes in both the cross-modal projector and the language model's LoRA adapters. In component restoration experiments, restoring an earlier task's LoRA adapter while retaining the final-task projector can leave an accuracy gap relative to restoring both components. To address these two sources of forgetting, we present \textbf{JoMe} (\textbf{Jo}int \textbf{Me}rging), which combines \textbf{C}ross-modal \textbf{P}rojection \textbf{M}erging (\textbf{CPM}) and \textbf{L}ow-rank \textbf{P}arameter \textbf{M}erging (\textbf{LPM}). Specifically, CPM recovers perceptual alignment by adaptively merging cross-modal visual representations via visual-prototype guidance during inference. Simultaneously, LPM recursively merges task-specific LoRA updates to mitigate interference across tasks. By leveraging recursive least squares, LPM yields a closed-form solution to the layer-wise least-squares objective on fixed inputs. Notably, JoMe operates as a training-free paradigm that achieves knowledge merging via efficient CPU-based algebraic operations, eliminating additional gradient-based optimization beyond initial tuning. Our extensive evaluations confirm the superior performance and robustness of JoMe across multiple MLLMs and benchmarks. Specifically, on the UCIT benchmark, JoMe achieves significant leads of up to 5.37\% and 1.72\% in final average accuracy over state-of-the-art methods across two different MLLMs, respectively. \footnote{Our code and data are included in the supplementary material for examination.}

2604.21903.title: A Scale-Adaptive Framework for Joint Spatiotemporal Super-Resolution with Diffusion Models
2604.21903.authors: Max Defez, Filippo Quarenghi, Mathieu Vrac, Stephan Mandt, Tom Beucler
2604.21903.abstract: Deep-learning video super-resolution has progressed rapidly, but climate applications typically super-resolve (increase resolution) either space or time, and joint spatiotemporal models are often designed for a single pair of super-resolution (SR) factors (upscaling spatial and temporal ratio between the low-resolution sequence and the high-resolution sequence), limiting transfer across spatial resolutions and temporal cadences (frame rates). We present a scale-adaptive framework that reuses the same architecture across factors by decomposing spatiotemporal SR into a deterministic prediction of the conditional mean, with attention, and a residual conditional diffusion model, with an optional mass-conservation (same precipitation amount in inputs and outputs) transform to preserve aggregated totals. Assuming that larger SR factors primarily increase underdetermination (hence required context and residual uncertainty) rather than changing the conditional-mean structure, scale adaptivity is achieved by retuning three factor-dependent hyperparameters before retraining: the diffusion noise schedule amplitude beta (larger for larger factors to increase diversity), the temporal context length L (set to maintain comparable attention horizons across cadences) and optionally a third, the mass-conservation function f (tapered to limit the amplification of extremes for large factors). Demonstrated on reanalysis precipitation over France (Comephore), the same architecture spans super-resolution factors from 1 to 25 in space and 1 to 6 in time, yielding a reusable architecture and tuning recipe for joint spatiotemporal super-resolution across scales.

2605.06615.title: When and Why SignSGD Outperforms SGD: A Theoretical Study Based on $\ell_1$-norm Lower Bounds
2605.06615.authors: Hongyi Tao, Dingzhi Yu, Lijun Zhang
2605.06615.abstract: Sign-based optimization algorithms, such as SignSGD and Muon, have garnered significant attention for their remarkable performance in training large foundation models. Despite this empirical success, we still lack a theoretical understanding of when and why these sign-based methods outperform vanilla SGD. The core obstacle is that under standard smoothness and finite variance conditions, SGD is known to be minimax optimal for finding stationary points measured by $\ell_2$-norms, thereby fundamentally precluding any complexity gains for sign-based methods in standard settings. To overcome this barrier, we analyze sign-based optimizers leveraging $\ell_1$-norm stationarity, $\ell_\infty$-smoothness, and a separable noise model, which can better capture the coordinate-wise nature of signed updates. Under this distinct problem geometry, we derive matched upper and lower bounds for SignSGD and explicitly characterize the problem class in which SignSGD provably dominates SGD. Specifically, we compare the upper bound of SignSGD with the lower bound of SGD, illustrating that SignSGD effectively reduces the complexity by a factor of $d$ under sparse noise, where $d$ is the problem dimension. Furthermore, we elevate this framework to the matrix domain, providing an equivalent optimal lower bound for the Muon optimizer, proving that extending the sign operator to matrices preserves this optimal scaling with dimensionality. Finally, we bridge our theoretical bounds to practice, demonstrating that the theoretical superiority of SignSGD accurately predicts its faster convergence during the pretraining of nanoGPT and LLaMA, with Muon also outperforming SGD in these experiments. Code is available at https://github.com/Dingzhen230/SignSGD_Outperforms_SGD.

2605.07719.title: Mosaic: Efficient CPU-GPU Coordinated Block-Sparse Attention
2605.07719.authors: Feiyu Yao, Zhixiong Niu, Xiaqing Li, Yongqiang Xiong, Juan Fang, Qian Wang
2605.07719.abstract: Long-context LLM serving increasingly relies on CPU-resident context KV cache, driven by KV offloading and disaggregated prefill--decode execution. Although block-sparse attention reduces KV access, existing designs remain inefficient: GPU-centralized execution fetches selected KV blocks from CPU memory at each decoding step, making it PCIe-bound, while CPU--GPU partitioned execution places CPU-side sparse attention on the critical path, leaving substantial GPU time idle. This paper presents Mosaic, a CPU--GPU coordinated block-sparse attention system for efficient long-context decoding with CPU-resident context KV. Mosaic builds on three key insights: output-contribution-aware KV budgeting, head-specific and granularity-aware sparse configuration, and cross-device coordinated scheduling for sparse tasks over CPU-resident KV. Guided by these insights, Mosaic integrates a lightweight head-property predictor, a granularity--budget selector, and a priority-based scheduler to automatically configure and coordinate sparse attention, preserving output quality while improving efficiency on heterogeneous architectures. Across 2 models, 3 benchmarks, and 40 tasks, Mosaic preserves near-FULL quality while achieving a better overall quality--efficiency tradeoff than the evaluated baselines. Compared with the best-quality fixed Quest configuration, Mosaic improves TPOT by up to 3.7$\times$. We further validate Mosaic across four hardware configurations and in a large-model multi-GPU deployment.

2605.08144.title: NoiseRater: Meta-Learned Noise Valuation for Diffusion Model Training
2605.08144.authors: Haokai Zhao, Da Xing, Hanqun Cao, Tinson Xu, Xinyu Xiang, Yanchao Li, Xiangru Tang, Hongbin Lin, Zehong Wang, Kuan Pang, Peng Xia, Molei Tao, Li Erran Li, Aditya Joshi, Jure Leskovec, Fang Wu
2605.08144.abstract: Training a diffusion model involves two sources of randomness for each data sample: the timestep and the Gaussian noise realization. The timestep has been studied extensively through scheduling and weighting, whereas the impact of the noise realization at a given timestep is still underexplored. In this work, we examine whether different noise instances are equally informative. We introduce NoiseRater, a network that scores an individual noise instance conditioned on the data sample and timestep. The rater is learned through bilevel optimization, where its scores reweight the diffusion loss in the inner loop, and it is updated to reduce validation loss after the inner-loop updates. Using the trained rater to select training noise, we observe three properties of training noise. First, noise realizations at the same timestep are not equally useful: the rater's top-scored noise improves performance over i.i.d. sampling, while its bottom-scored noise degrades it. Second, this utility is contextual: it depends most strongly on the timestep, and to a lesser extent on the image and the class label. Third, noise selection is complementary to timestep-level design, retaining most of its gain when combined with existing scheduling and weighting schemes. These findings establish instance-level noise valuation as a new axis for understanding and improving diffusion training. Code is available at https://github.com/JoeZhao527/Noise-Rater.

2605.11229.title: Comment and Control: Hijacking Agentic Workflows via Context-Grounded Evolution
2605.11229.authors: Neil Fendley, Zhengyu Liu, Aonan Guan, Jiacheng Zhong, Yinzhi Cao
2605.11229.abstract: Automation platforms such as GitHub Actions and n8n are increasingly adopting so-called agentic workflows, which integrate Large Language Model (LLM) agents for tasks such as code review and data synchronization. While bringing convenience for developers, this integration exposes a new risk: An adversary may control and craft certain inputs, such as GitHub issue comments, to manipulate the LLM agent for unwanted actions, such as credential exfiltration and arbitrary command execution. To our knowledge, no prior academic work has studied such a risk in agentic workflows. In this paper, we design the first detection and exploitation framework, called JAW, to hijack agentic workflows hosted on automation platforms via a novel approach called Context-Grounded Evolution. Our key idea is to evolve agentic workflow inputs under the contexts derived from hybrid program analysis for hijacking purposes. Specifically, JAW generates agentic workflow contexts through three analyses: (i) static path-feasibility analysis to identify feasible agent-invocation paths and the input constraints required to trigger them, (ii) dynamic prompt-provenance analysis to determine how that input is transformed and embedded into the LLM context, and (iii) capability analysis to identify the actions and restrictions available to the agent at runtime. Our evaluation of JAW on GitHub workflows and n8n templates showed that 4714 GitHub workflows and eight n8n templates can be successfully hijacked, for example, to leak user credentials. Our findings span 15 widely-used GitHub Actions, including official GitHub Actions for Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Qwen CLI, and Cursor CLI, and two official n8n nodes. We responsibly disclosed all findings to the affected vendors and received many acknowledgements, fixes, and bug bounties, notably from GitHub, Google, and Anthropic.

2605.14269.title: PhyMotion: Structured 3D Motion Reward for Physics-Grounded Human Video Generation
2605.14269.authors: Yidong Huang, Zun Wang, Han Lin, Dong-Ki Kim, Shayegan Omidshafiei, Jaehong Yoon, Jaemin Cho, Yue Zhang, Mohit Bansal
2605.14269.abstract: Generating realistic human motion is a central yet unsolved challenge in video generation. While reinforcement learning (RL)-based post-training has driven recent gains in general video quality, extending it to human motion remains bottlenecked by a reward signal that cannot reliably score motion realism. Existing video rewards primarily rely on 2D perceptual signals, without explicitly modeling the 3D body state, contact, and dynamics underlying articulated human motion, and often assign high scores to videos with floating bodies or physically implausible movements. To address this, we propose PhyMotion, a structured, fine-grained motion reward that grounds recovered 3D human trajectories in a physics simulator and evaluates motion quality along multiple dimensions of physical feasibility. Concretely, we recover SMPL body meshes from generated videos, retarget them onto a humanoid in the MuJoCo physics simulator, and evaluate the resulting motion along three axes: kinematic plausibility, contact and balance consistency, and dynamic feasibility. Each component provides a continuous and interpretable signal tied to a specific aspect of motion quality, allowing the reward to capture which aspects of motion are physically correct or violated. Experiments show that PhyMotion achieves stronger correlation with human judgments than existing reward formulations. These gains carry over to RL-based post-training, where optimizing PhyMotion leads to larger and more consistent improvements than optimizing existing rewards, improving motion realism across both autoregressive and bidirectional video generators under both automatic metrics and blind human evaluation (+68 Elo gain). Ablations show that the three axes provide complementary supervision signals, while the reward preserves overall video generation quality with only modest training overhead.

2605.16381.title: StreamPro: Reinforcement Learning with Multi-Grained Rewards for Proactive Streaming Video Understanding
2605.16381.authors: Ao Li, Zihan Xiao, Zihao Yue, Boshen Xu, Linli Yao, Jiaze Li, Pei Fu, Jianzhong Ju, Jian Luan, Qin Jin
2605.16381.abstract: Proactive streaming video understanding requires models to continuously monitor evolving video streams and decide whether, when, and what to respond. However, training models with such proactive capabilities remains challenging. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) suffers from severe imbalance between silence and response signals, while reinforcement learning (RL) faces sparse response-level rewards and difficulties in optimizing interdependent response sequences. To address these challenges, we propose StreamPro, a two-stage training framework. We first introduce CB-Stream Loss to alleviate supervision imbalance during SFT. We then employ Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with two complementary rewards: a refined Response-Matching (RM) reward that provides denser feedback for individual response decisions, and a rubric-based Sequence-Quality (SQ) reward that encourages globally coherent response sequences. To support the two training stages, we construct StreamPro-SFT-63K and StreamPro-RL-3K, respectively. To address the limited task coverage of existing proactive benchmarks, we further introduce StreamPro-Bench, encompassing three task categories: Perceptual Understanding, Temporal Reasoning, and Anticipatory Assistance, along with StreamPro-F1 to evaluate response correctness, timing, and frequency. Experiments demonstrate that StreamPro substantially improves proactive streaming video understanding, achieving an average StreamPro-F1 of 32.8 on StreamPro-Bench, compared with 9.2 for the strongest baseline, while maintaining strong performance on real-time streaming tasks, reaching 79.8 on StreamingBench-RTVU.

2605.22414.title: Towards Clinically Interpretable Ophthalmic VQA via Spatially-Grounded Lesion Evidence
2605.22414.authors: Xingyue Wang, Bo Liu, Meng Wang, Zhixuan Zhang, Chengcheng Zhu, Huazhu Fu, Jiang Liu
2605.22414.abstract: Visual Question Answering (VQA) holds great promise for clinical support, particularly in ophthalmology, where retinal fundus photography is essential for diagnosis. However, ophthalmic VQA benchmarks primarily emphasize answer accuracy, neglecting the explicit visual evidence necessary for clinical interpretability. In this work, we introduce FundusGround, a new benchmark for clinically interpretable ophthalmic VQA with spatially-grounded lesion evidence. Specifically, we propose a three-stage pipeline that collects 10,719 fundus images with 15,595 image-level meticulously annotated lesions. To ensure anatomical consistency and clinical validity, all lesions are spatially localized using the Early Treatment Diabetic Retinopathy Study (ETDRS) grid, enabling standardized mapping to nine clinically meaningful retinal regions. Built upon this structured lesion evidence, 72,706 questions are then generated spanning four formats: open-ended, closed-ended, single-choice, and multiple-choice. We further benchmark multiple general- and medical- large vision-language models using dual metrics for answer accuracy and lesion-level reasoning. The experiments demonstrate that incorporating lesion-level visual evidence consistently improves model performance and transparency, highlighting the necessity of explicit spatial grounding for reliable and explainable ophthalmic VQA.

2605.26179.title: AutoDFT: A Closed-Loop Multi-Agent Framework for Autonomous DFT Calculations
2605.26179.authors: Penghui Yang, Zhonghan Zhang, Yue Li, Xinrun Wang, Yanchen Deng, Yuhao Lu, Bijun Tang, Zheng Liu, Bo An
2605.26179.abstract: Density functional theory (DFT) serves as the basis for computational discovery in materials science and chemistry, yet each calculation demands extensive human effort: adjusting algorithms when convergence stalls, revising plans when unexpected physics emerges, and inserting steps as intermediate results reshape the problem. Existing LLM-based agents automate only the initial planning stage, producing a full execution plan upfront and leaving all subsequent adaptation to hand-crafted rules. As a result, these workflows remain fragile, do not generalize well beyond pre-planned scenarios, and often require expert intervention when failures or unexpected intermediate results require changes to the calculation path. Here, we introduce AutoDFT, a closed-loop multi-agent framework that embeds LLM reasoning into every stage of the DFT lifecycle, where a strategic planner produces a skeletal plan of step objectives; a step planner generates numerical parameters just in time from preceding results; and a monitor-recover-reflect cycle diagnoses failures, repairs them, and revises the plan when the evidence justifies it. We demonstrate both breadth and depth: breadth on VASPBench, a purpose-built benchmark spanning 34 tasks and 9 DFT calculation types, where AutoDFT achieves 94.1% task-level success with GPT-5.2; and depth on established materials databases, where AutoDFT produces quantitatively reliable property predictions across electronic, magnetic, and energetic properties. By closing the loop between planning and execution, AutoDFT enables experimentalists without deep computational expertise to obtain reliable first-principles results. Our code is available at https://github.com/penghui-yang/AutoDFT.

2605.27079.title: Trust Region Q Adjoint Matching
2605.27079.authors: Yonghoon Dong, Kyungmin Lee, Changyeon Kim, Jaehyuk Kim, Jinwoo Shin
2605.27079.abstract: Off-policy reinforcement learning of pretrained flow policies remains challenging due to the instability of optimization arising from the multi-step sampling process. Recently, Q-learning with Adjoint Matching (QAM) addressed this by recasting policy improvement as a stochastic optimal control (SOC) problem guided by a learned critic. However, QAM inherits a fundamental fragility of critic-guided improvement, since small critic errors can be exponentially amplified and often lead to performance collapse. This paper introduces Trust Region Q Adjoint Matching (TRQAM), a stable off-policy fine-tuning algorithm that adaptively controls the path-space KL between the fine-tuned and pretrained policies through projected dual descent. Specifically, we adapt a trust-region parameter $\lambda$ inside the sampling process of the flow policy and prove that $\lambda$ exactly weights the path-space KL in the SOC objective. As a result, our method can tightly control the deviation from the pretrained policy within a prescribed KL budget, achieving stable off-policy RL. Through experiments on 50 OGBench tasks, TRQAM consistently outperforms prior methods in both offline RL and offline-to-online RL. In particular, TRQAM achieves an overall success rate of 68% in offline RL, substantially improving over the strongest baseline at 46%.

2605.27380.title: BioELX: Context-Aware Cross-lingual Biomedical Entity Linking without Task-Specific Supervision
2605.27380.authors: Yi Wang, Corina Dima, Liangyu Zhong, Steffen Staab
2605.27380.abstract: Cross-lingual biomedical entity linking (BEL) maps mentions in any language to unique identifiers in a biomedical knowledge base, supporting clinical and biomedical NLP applications. We identify two issues affecting current systems. First, the UMLS (Bodenreider,2004) aliases used to train cross-lingual BEL retrievers are heavily skewed toward English, so retrievers generalize poorly to non-English mentions. Second, although context is often necessary for disambiguation, naively injecting context into retrievers trained only to align aliases severely degrades retrieval. We propose BioELX, a retrieve-rerank framework that addresses both issues. For retrieval, we continue training SapBERT_multi (Liu et al., 2021b) using Wikidata-derived cross-lingual alias supervision, forming shared concept neighborhoods across languages. For reranking, we adapt pretrained LLM rerankers to entity linking through mention-anchored prompting, which marks the target mention so that rerankers score candidates with respect to the intended mention rather than other salient tokens in the context. Experiments show that BioELX achieves new state-of-the-art results on four cross-lingual BEL benchmarks, improving Recall@1 by 4.9 to 18.2 percentage points over prior best results, without any task-specific BEL annotations. Our code and resources are available at https://github.com/AI4MedCode/BioELX.

2605.31094.title: Redefining Instance Matching: A Unified Framework for Part-Aware Matching in Panoptic Segmentation Evaluation
2605.31094.authors: Erik Gro{\ss}kopf, Soumya Snigdha Kundu, Hendrik M\"oller, Nicolas M\"unster, Mehdi Astaraki, Paula Tamara Buzduga, Kerstin Ritter, Benedikt Wiestler, Jan Kirschke, Jonathan Shapey, Tom Vercauteren, Florian Kofler
2605.31094.abstract: The Panoptic Quality metric is the standard for jointly evaluating instance and semantic segmentation. Its original definition matches predicted and ground truth segments only if their intersection over union exceeds 0.5, a threshold that guarantees a One-to-One matching that is both optimal and unique. Below this threshold, the uniqueness guarantee is lost and multiple matching strategies emerge in a poorly explored problem space. We systematically elucidate this space by recasting segment matching as a constrained bipartite assignment problem. Independently bounding the prediction- and ground-truth-side degrees yields four matching strategies: One-to-One, Many-to-One, One-to-Many, and Many-to-Many. We show that the first three yield interpretable instance-level assignments, whereas Many-to-Many entangles over- and under-segmentation and admits no consistent attribution of errors. These strategies become relevant when instances are fragmented, adjacent objects are difficult to delineate, or annotations are noisy. Central to our framework is a vertex-based accounting of TP, FP, and FN, anchored to ground truth and predicted segments rather than to matching edges. We further show that the framework extends naturally to part-aware panoptic segmentation and illustrate this extension conceptually on biomedical examples. Across configurable case studies we report how different combinations of thresholds and matching strategies behave in practice.

2606.02522.title: Moment-Video: Diagnosing Temporal Fidelity of Video MLLMs on Momentary Visual Events
